CBP's new tariff refund system risks leaving thousands of American companies with far less than they're legally owed, Cato scholars warn. 

They break down the good, the bad, and what we still don't know: 
ow.ly/JSoE50YOf4W

AI isn’t just tech—it’s becoming an extension of our work, ideas, and livelihoods. 

That means it deserves strong protections from government overreach. The freedom to build, create, and innovate are especially important to safeguard. Learn more from @KevinTFrazier.
ow.ly/gT8J50YO2Jm

The FBI just conceded in court it did investigate the Cato Institute and its employees—after telling Cato in 2019 it had “no records.” Now the question is whether it’s still ongoing, as Congress debates FISA Section 702 and FBI surveillance powers, reports @PGEddington. ow.ly/s1Jr50YOeR3

There's strong evidence that rules-based monetary policy improves economic outcomes, says Cato's @JaiKedia. When the Fed follows a rule, the scope for political interference shrinks significantly.

Video

Our brains evolved for small-group, zero-sum competition—not vast markets among strangers. That mismatch helps explain why policies like rent control and tariffs stay popular despite poor economic results, argues Cato’s Adam Omary. 

ow.ly/ouvv50YO8hX

The Trump administration has slashed green card approvals by about half, reports Cato’s @David_J_Bier. 

The steepest cuts have fallen on humanitarian categories — asylees, refugees, Cubans, and other (mostly crime victims).

Kevin Warsh’s confirmation hearing before the Senate banking Committee put affordability on center stage. There were encouraging signs but also some important policy prescriptions left undiscussed, says Cato’s @JaiKedia. 

ow.ly/2MP150YOaH1

The government blocked Spirit's private merger, then helped create the fuel crisis now threatening it. Now a federal equity stake is on the table—a case study in how each government intervention becomes the rationale for the next intervention, explains Cato’s @DeHavenTad.

ow.ly/ryjr50YO4qu

Nearly 200 automated license plate cameras in Norfolk log where and when cars travel—then store that data for 21 days. Cato argues this warrantless tracking of daily movements is unconstitutional under the Fourth Amendment. 

Learn more: ow.ly/8Y1x50YO4as

After its “emergency” tariffs were struck down, the Trump admin launched new “Section 301” probes that raise big concerns. Their economic case looks weak and rushed, and officials say the outcomes have already been decided: tariffs will be back by summer. This looks more like a legal workaround than a real investigation. Cato's @scottlincicome and Chad Smitson explain:
ow.ly/NzZ850YO2iS

If the goal is to lower prices or broaden options of life’s essential goods and services, the answer is not price controls, subsidies, and mandates. It is more economic freedom to supply.  

The Cato Institute “Handbook on Affordability” features 100+ policy ideas to defuse inflation and lower the cost of living: ow.ly/wssl50YLhxF

President Trump’s reasons for quitting NATO may miss the alliance’s rules—but the policy case remains: NATO outlived its Cold War purpose, the US pays disproportionately, and the commitments can bypass Congress. Cato’s @MWChapman argues it’s time to withdraw. ow.ly/g81L50YNu0H

Hillary Clinton recently outlined a proposal to make childcare affordable, but subsidies don't make it cheaper to provide—they mainly just shift the bill to taxpayers. Real affordability means removing  regulations that drive costs up, Cato’s @MrRBourne explains.

ow.ly/Azj150YN9KH

The Supreme Court heard a major case today on whether the FCC can impose $100M+ in penalties without a jury trial. Cato’s amicus brief argued this violates the Seventh Amendment—agencies shouldn't be judge, jury, and enforcer of their own claims. 

Read more: ow.ly/vtuF50YNEIr

Congress imposed strict limits on refrigerant production but let the EPA decide who gets to produce—handing an agency a power that belongs to Congress. SCOTUS should revive nondelegation and make Congress own the hard choices, argue Cato’s Thomas A. Berry, Brent Skorup, and Alexander Xenos. 

Learn more: ow.ly/v8LE50YNyaO

Virginia joined the National Popular Vote Compact—but the plan still has legal and practical gaps. Even after recent reforms, questions remain about recount rules, dispute resolution, and whether courts would enforce the compact. 

Learn more: ow.ly/uF5050YMU3F

Calling heavy social media use “addiction” is fueling lawsuits and new laws built on weak scientific foundation. Cato’s @dr4liberty and @AdamOmaryPhD say we’re mixing up habit, dependence, and true addiction, which could have major consequences for privacy, free speech, and innovation.

ow.ly/xtof50YMIY1
